procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam dated 4th March 2024 in Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 1271 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant approached the Kerala High Court by way of a habeas corpus petition (Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 1271 of 2023) challenging the detention of the detenu. The High Court rejected the writ petition by its judgment and order dated 4th March 2024.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, being aggrieved by the High Court's decision, approached the Supreme Court by way of a Special Leave Petition, which was converted into Criminal Appeal No. 3083 of 2024. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing and setting aside the High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court also noted that the order of detention was a colourable act as the petitioner was already in jail.

decision.conviction_status: Detention order quashed and set aside.
directions: The judgment and order of the High Court dated 4th March 2024 in Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 1271 of 2023 is quashed and set aside.
The order dated 31st August 2023 passed by the Joint Secretary (COFEPOSA) to the Government of India directing the detention of the detenu is quashed and set aside.

The order dated 28th November 2023 passed by the Under Secretary, COFEPOSA Wing, Central Economic Intelligence Bureau, Department of Revenue, Ministry of Revenue, Government of India is quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned detention order was passed without application of mind?

law.law_text: A detention order is unsustainable if the Detaining Authority has not applied their mind to the material in a proper perspective.
The material against a detenu must be such that it could lead a reasonable person to conclude that a detention order is necessary.

application.fact_or_law: The petitioner's counsel argued that the material against the detenu could not have led any reasonable person to conclude that there was a case for detention.
application.applied_to: The counsel contended that this demonstrated the Detaining Authority had not applied its mind to the material in the proper perspective.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's argument, concluding that the Detaining Authority had passed the detention order without a proper application of mind, which resulted in an unsustainable order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grounds for the detention order are vague?

facts: The detention order was based on 12 grounds.
The Detaining Authority relied on various materials to arrive at its subjective satisfaction.
law: Under section 5A of the COFEPOSA, if a detention order is made on several grounds, it can be sustained on the valid grounds even if one or more of the other grounds are found to be vitiated.
The Supreme Court distinguishes between a detention order passed on various distinct grounds and an order passed on one ground that relies on various materials.
application: The Court questioned whether the materials relied upon by the Detaining Authority for its subjective satisfaction could be severed in the same way that distinct grounds can be.

The Court considered that if a detention order is based on several factual aspects (materials), and some of those materials are flawed or not supplied, it is uncertain whether the Detaining Authority would have reached the same subjective satisfaction without them.
This inability to sever the underlying materials from the grounds of detention casts doubt on the validity of the entire order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the grounds for detention were vague by challenging the foundation of the Detaining Authority's 'subjective satisfaction'. It reasoned that when an order relies on multiple pieces of material, and some of that material is flawed, the entire basis for the detention becomes uncertain and invalid, as it's impossible to know if the authority would have issued the order based only on the remaining, valid material.

cases.case_name: M. Ahamedkutty vs. Union of India and another
cases.principle: It is imperative that every document which has been relied on by the Detaining Authority and which affects the right of the detenu to make an effective representation under Article 22(5) has to be supplied to the detenu.

cases.case_name: L.M.S. Ummu Saleema v. B.B. Gujaral
cases.principle: It is only the failure to furnish copies of such documents as were relied upon by the detaining authority, making it difficult for the detenu to make an effective representation, that amounts to a violation of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 22(5).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is a constitutional imperative for a detaining authority to provide the detenu with all documents relied upon and referred to in the detention order, simultaneously with the grounds of detention. These relied-upon documents form an inseparable basis for the detention, and a failure to provide them vitiates the entire detention order, as the materials considered by the authority cannot be severed.
obiter: Any unexplained slackness by the government in promptly considering a detenu's representation against a detention order constitutes a denial of statutory protection and results in the invalidation of the order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's core finding is that the detention order is invalid due to a breach of the constitutional imperatives outlined in Article 22(5). The failure to provide the detenu with all documents referred to or relied upon in the grounds of detention rendered those grounds incomplete. This procedural lapse denied the detenu the constitutionally guaranteed right to make an effective representation against the detention, thereby vitiating the entire detention order.
legal_tests_applied: The constitutional imperatives in Article 22(5) are twofold: (1) The detaining authority must, as soon as practicable, communicate to the detenu the grounds on which the order of detention has been made, and (2) the detaining authority must afford the detenu the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order of detention.

The right to make an effective representation requires that the detenu be furnished with the grounds of detention along with all documents referred to or relied on. If there is a failure or delay in furnishing these documents, it amounts to a denial of the right to make an effective representation.

While issuing a detention order, the detaining authority must be provided with all available materials concerning the individual, both inculpatory and exculpatory, to enable it to reach a just conclusion about the necessity of detention.
policy_considerations: In matters of preventive detention, the obligation of the detaining authority under Article 22(5) to allow a detenu the earliest opportunity to make a representation and to consider that representation speedily is a fundamental constitutional imperative.

The consistent view of the Supreme Court is that a representation from a detenu must be considered with reasonable expedition, as this is a crucial safeguard against the arbitrary deprivation of liberty.
